title: How to get a perfect 50/50 from a bent coin
description:
A coin that lands heads 70% of the time can still settle a bet fairly. Flip it twice: two heads or two tails, throw the pair away; heads then tails means heads, tails then heads means tails. Both orders have the same chance, 70% x 30% = 21%, so the bias cancels exactly, even if you don't know how bent the coin is. The price is time: only 42% of pairs count, so each answer takes about 5 flips (1 / (p x (1 - p)) on average). John von Neumann described the trick in 1951.

Numbers checked in code: every figure computed, plus 200,000 simulated answers each for a 70% coin, a 90% coin and coins of random unknown bias (all came out 50/50 within half a percent). Source: Wikipedia, Fair coin (von Neumann, 1951).

facts_checked: 70% heads: HT = TH = 0.7 x 0.3 = 21%, HH 49%, TT 9%; 42% of pairs count; 1 / (0.7 x 0.3) = 4.76 flips per answer (about 5); CTA 90% coin: 1 / 0.09 = 11.1 flips (verify.py)
Simulation: 200,000 answers each for a 70% coin (heads 0.501, 4.77 flips), a 90% coin (0.499, 11.09 flips) and random unknown bias (0.498): all fair (verify.py)

Von Neumann's procedure: toss twice, discard HH/TT, keep the first of HT/TH; fair because the two orders are equally likely; expected flips 1 / (p(1-p)); J. von Neumann, 'Various techniques used in connection with random digits', NBS Applied Math Series 12 (1951) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_coin)

beats.say: Your bent coin or a fair one: both give fifty-fifty.
You don't fix the coin. You don't even need to know how bent it is.
Your coin lands heads 70% of the time. Call tails, and you lose 7 times in 10.
So flip it twice, not once.
Two heads or two tails? Throw that pair away and flip again.
Heads then tails counts as heads. Tails then heads counts as tails.
But the coin still loves heads. So how is that fair?
Heads then tails: 70% times 30%, that's 21%. Tails then heads: 30% times 70%. The same 21%.
The price is time. Only 42% of pairs count, so each answer takes about 5 flips.
Any coin, bent any way, becomes a perfect fifty-fifty. John von Neumann wrote this down in 1951.
